questions.explanation: A promise not to sell the records can hold while categories inferred from what someone reads still reach advertising partners, so the literal claim and the real behaviour are different questions. Declaring the claim false for any derived signal treats a narrow promise as if it covered all sharing, and accepting a true narrow claim as settling everything leaves the sharing unexamined.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim literally covers, and what the same page admits happens.
questions.learningObjective: separate a narrow vendor claim from the behaviour described elsewhere

options.misconception: treats a literal claim as settling every sharing question
options.text: The literal claim may hold, while what is inferred is shared onward
The narrow claim holds, and inferred interests still reach partners

options.misconception: insists any derived signal must be the literal record itself
options.text: The claim is false, because inferred interests count as personal data

options.misconception: reads a promise not to sell as a promise of no sharing at all
options.text: The claim is false, since any sharing at all breaks the promise given

questions.explanation: A rate that roughly tripled while enrolment held steady is a change worth investigating, but two before-and-after totals cannot establish what caused it, so the honest reading pairs suspicion with a check. A change in timing is not proof of cause, comparing 41 against a whole population's worth of students measures the wrong denominator, and the table states enrolment stayed flat.
questions.hint: Ask what the table can and cannot show about why the number moved.
questions.learningObjective: draw a bounded conclusion from a before-and-after harm table

options.text: The rise followed the change and merits a look, but cause is not shown

options.misconception: treats a change in timing as proof of causation
options.text: The app caused the rise, since the number rose right after it arrived

options.misconception: dismisses a tripled rate by comparing it to a whole population
options.text: Nothing is wrong, since 41 students is small beside all the pupils

options.misconception: invents a change the table explicitly says did not happen
options.text: Enrolment rose over the period and explains the larger number found

questions.explanation: Access is conditional on accepting monitoring, so the 1,200 who decline are exactly the people the rule shuts out, and 5,000 minus 1,200 leaves 3,800 still able to use the service. Counting the 1,200 answers with the excluded rather than the included, and keeping the full 5,000 forgets that the service was not actually open to all of them.
questions.hint: Subtract the people who fail the condition from the people eligible.
questions.learningObjective: compute who keeps access when a benefit is conditioned on monitoring

questions.explanation: Nobody has measured the error rate, so a trial in one clinic with checks produces the missing evidence and keeps the decision reversible, which is what an unmeasured tool warrants. Staff support does not make a patient objection minor, and reading unmeasured as disproved throws away a test that would settle the question, while clinician preference alone is not the consent the patients gave.
questions.hint: Ask what is missing, and which course would produce it without making the decision permanent.
questions.learningObjective: choose a bounded trial over blanket adoption or blanket refusal

options.misconception: lets staff support outweigh a patient objection outright
options.text: Adopt it across the hospital, since staff support outweighs any objection

options.misconception: reads unmeasured as disproved and rules out any test
options.text: Refuse it permanently, since an unmeasured tool cannot be a safe one
Trial it in one clinic with error checks, then decide from findings

options.misconception: treats clinician preference as the only consent that counts
options.text: Adopt it wherever a clinician asks for it, letting each decide alone

questions.explanation: A defensible judgement states the purpose, confirms the benefit is real, names everyone exposed, sizes the harm, asks whether it can be undone, and only then chooses an action with the condition for reversing it attached. Counting an assumed benefit as confirmed and leaving reversibility to the end both settle questions the order needs answered first.
questions.hint: Start with the purpose, and end with the action and its reversal condition.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a defensible benefit-and-harm weighing

options.misconception: starts weighing harms before stating the purpose at all
options.text: State plainly what the feature is for and who asked for it

options.misconception: counts an assumed benefit as a confirmed one
options.text: Name who gains, and check the gain is real rather than assumed

options.misconception: lists only the people who agreed to take part
options.text: Name who is exposed, including those who never chose this

options.misconception: judges a harm without ever sizing it
options.text: Estimate how large the harm is and how badly it lands

options.misconception: asks about reversibility only after the harm occurred
options.text: Check whether the action can be undone if the harm proves real

options.misconception: commits to an action with no condition for changing course
options.text: Choose the action, and name the check that would reverse it
